metadata.title: The File Is the Program.
metadata.subtitle: The Skill Development Skill
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when you build a Claude Skill, are you writing code Claude executes, or something else? Lands the carry-out that a Skill is plain instructions Claude reads and follows itself, so it only ever does exactly what the file's words say.

beats.narration_text: People come to this thinking a Skill is code Claude executes — a program you write, that Claude runs. Wrong model. A Skill is a text file Claude reads and acts on. No compiler, no runtime beneath it. So: how do you write one?

beats.narration_text: Here is what is actually happening. A skill is a folder Claude reads before it works. This one is skill-development — the skill for building skills. Inside: one SKILL.md file, about twenty-two kilobytes, and a references folder next to it. The SKILL.md holds the entire instruction set, written in plain English, with no hidden runtime underneath it. Claude reads the file, then acts on what the words say. That is why we say the file is the program — the design choice here is that the instructions and the executable are the same object.

Two things have to hit before any of this runs. First, the SKILL.md carries a description saying when the skill applies — for this one, that is when you want to create a skill, add one to a plugin, write a new one, improve a skill's description, organize its content, or get guidance on skill structure. When your request matches that description, Claude reads the file. Then it executes the Steps section in order, top to bottom — linear, no branching unless a step explicitly says so. The design choice is legibility: the trigger is human-readable text, not a compiled predicate. You can audit exactly when the skill fires by reading English.

production_viz.label: HOW IT GETS PICKED UP
production_viz.caption: only runs when the words match

beats.narration_text: Because it is plain instructions and not code, skill-development runs the same way on the same request every time. Repeatable, not improvised — same words in, same execution out. But that reliability has a matching cost. Nothing hidden fills in for what the file does not cover. Ask for something the SKILL.md never describes, and there is no fallback logic underneath to catch you. The file's words are the entire boundary of what happens. They optimized for auditability at the expense of graceful degradation.

production_viz.label: ONLY WHAT'S WRITTEN
production_viz.caption: the file's words are the boundary

beats.narration_text: A Skill is not code Claude runs. It is plain instructions Claude reads and follows itself. So it only ever does exactly what the words on the page say — nothing more, and nothing hidden.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want to write my first Claude Skill for a workflow I actually do — replying to customer support emails in my product's voice. Help me draft the SKILL.md. Walk me through what belongs in the description field so Claude picks the skill up at the right time, what belongs in the Steps section so it runs the same way each time, and what belongs in a references folder next to it. Then hand me the SKILL.md as plain markdown I can drop in a folder and try. Go deeper: ask the same model where your first draft will silently fail — which request phrasings will match your description but land on a step you never wrote — and how to close that gap without adding hidden fallback logic.
